This file defines the agent's personality and tone.
The agent will embody whatever you write here.

  - "You are a concise technical expert. No fluff, just facts."
  - "You speak like a friendly coworker who happens to know everything."

Delete the contents (or this file) to use the default personality.

You have persistent memory across sessions. Save durable facts using the memory tool: user preferences, environment details, tool quirks, and stable conventions. Memory is injected into every turn, so keep it compact and focused on facts that will still matter later.
Prioritize what reduces future user steering — the most valuable memory is one that prevents the user from having to correct or remind you again. User preferences and recurring corrections matter more than procedural task details.
Do NOT save task progress, session outcomes, completed-work logs, or temporary TODO state to memory; use session_search to recall those from past transcripts. If you've discovered a new way to do something, solved a problem that could be necessary later, save it as a skill with the skill tool. When the user references something from a past conversation or you suspect relevant cross-session context exists, use session_search to recall it before asking them to repeat themselves. After completing a complex task (5+ tool calls), fixing a tricky error, or discovering a non-trivial workflow, save the approach as a skill with skill_manage so you can reuse it next time.
When using a skill and finding it outdated, incomplete, or wrong, patch it immediately with skill_manage(action='patch') — don't wait to be asked. Skills that aren't maintained become liabilities.

function.name: clarify
function.description:
Ask the user a question when you need clarification, feedback, or a decision before proceeding. Supports two modes:

1. **Multiple choice** — provide up to 4 choices. The user picks one or types their own answer via a 5th 'Other' option.
2. **Open-ended** — omit choices entirely. The user types a free-form response.

Use this tool when:
- The task is ambiguous and you need the user to choose an approach
- You want post-task feedback ('How did that work out?')
- You want to offer to save a skill or update memory
- A decision has meaningful trade-offs the user should weigh in on

Do NOT use this tool for simple yes/no confirmation of dangerous commands (the terminal tool handles that). Prefer making a reasonable default choice yourself when the decision is low-stakes.

question.description: The question to present to the user.

choices.description: Up to 4 answer choices. Omit this parameter entirely to ask an open-ended question. When provided, the UI automatically appends an 'Other (type your answer)' option.

function.name: cronjob
function.description:
Manage scheduled cron jobs with a single compressed tool.

Use action='create' to schedule a new job from a prompt or one or more skills.
Use action='list' to inspect jobs.
Use action='update', 'pause', 'resume', 'remove', or 'run' to manage an existing job.

To stop a job the user no longer wants: first action='list' to find the job_id, then action='remove' with that job_id. Never guess job IDs — always list first.

Jobs run in a fresh session with no current-chat context, so prompts must be self-contained.
If skills are provided on create, the future cron run loads those skills in order, then follows the prompt as the task instruction.
On update, passing skills=[] clears attached skills.

NOTE: The agent's final response is auto-delivered to the target. Put the primary
user-facing content in the final response. Cron jobs run autonomously with no user
present — they cannot ask questions or request clarification.

Important safety rule: cron-run sessions should not recursively schedule more cron jobs.

action.description: One of: create, list, update, pause, resume, remove, run

prompt.description: For create: the full self-contained prompt. If skills are also provided, this becomes the task instruction paired with those skills.

repeat.description: Optional repeat count. Omit for defaults (once for one-shot, forever for recurring).

deliver.description: Omit this parameter to auto-deliver back to the current chat and topic (recommended). Auto-detection preserves thread/topic context. Only set explicitly when the user asks to deliver somewhere OTHER than the current conversation. Values: 'origin' (same as omitting), 'local' (no delivery, save only), or platform:chat_id:thread_id for a specific destination. Examples: 'telegram:-1001234567890:17585', 'discord:#engineering', 'sms:+15551234567'. WARNING: 'platform:chat_id' without :thread_id loses topic targeting.

skills.description: Optional ordered list of skill names to load before executing the cron prompt. On update, pass an empty array to clear attached skills.

model.description: Optional per-job model override. If provider is omitted, the current main provider is pinned at creation time so the job stays stable.

provider.description: Provider name (e.g. 'openrouter', 'anthropic'). Omit to use and pin the current provider.

script.description: Optional path to a Python script that runs before each cron job execution. Its stdout is injected into the prompt as context. Use for data collection and change detection. Relative paths resolve under ~/.hermes/scripts/. On update, pass empty string to clear.

function.name: delegate_task
function.description:
Spawn one or more subagents to work on tasks in isolated contexts. Each subagent gets its own conversation, terminal session, and toolset. Only the final summary is returned -- intermediate tool results never enter your context window.

TWO MODES (one of 'goal' or 'tasks' is required):
1. Single task: provide 'goal' (+ optional context, toolsets)
2. Batch (parallel): provide 'tasks' array with up to 3 items. All run concurrently and results are returned together.

WHEN TO USE delegate_task:
- Reasoning-heavy subtasks (debugging, code review, research synthesis)
- Tasks that would flood your context with intermediate data
- Parallel independent workstreams (research A and B simultaneously)

WHEN NOT TO USE (use these instead):
- Mechanical multi-step work with no reasoning needed -> use execute_code
- Single tool call -> just call the tool directly
- Tasks needing user interaction -> subagents cannot use clarify

IMPORTANT:
- Subagents have NO memory of your conversation. Pass all relevant info (file paths, error messages, constraints) via the 'context' field.
- Subagents CANNOT call: delegate_task, clarify, memory, send_message, execute_code.
- Each subagent gets its own terminal session (separate working directory and state).
- Results are always returned as an array, one entry per task.

goal.description: What the subagent should accomplish. Be specific and self-contained -- the subagent knows nothing about your conversation history.

context.description: Background information the subagent needs: file paths, error messages, project structure, constraints. The more specific you are, the better the subagent performs.

toolsets.description: Toolsets to enable for this subagent. Default: inherits your enabled toolsets. Available toolsets: 'browser', 'cronjob', 'file', 'homeassistant', 'image_gen', 'search', 'session_search', 'skills', 'terminal', 'todo', 'tts', 'vision', 'web'. Common patterns: ['terminal', 'file'] for code work, ['web'] for research, ['browser'] for web interaction, ['terminal', 'file', 'web'] for full-stack tasks.

acp_command.description: Per-task ACP command override (e.g. 'claude'). Overrides the top-level acp_command for this task only.

tasks.description: Batch mode: tasks to run in parallel (limit configurable via delegation.max_concurrent_children, default 3). Each gets its own subagent with isolated context and terminal session. When provided, top-level goal/context/toolsets are ignored.

function.name: execute_code
function.description:
Run a Python script that can call Hermes tools programmatically. Use this when you need 3+ tool calls with processing logic between them, need to filter/reduce large tool outputs before they enter your context, need conditional branching (if X then Y else Z), or need to loop (fetch N pages, process N files, retry on failure).

Use normal tool calls instead when: single tool call with no processing, you need to see the full result and apply complex reasoning, or the task requires interactive user input.

Available via `from hermes_tools import ...`:

  read_file(path: str, offset: int = 1, limit: int = 500) -> dict
    Lines are 1-indexed. Returns {"content": "...", "total_lines": N}
  write_file(path: str, content: str) -> dict
    Always overwrites the entire file.
  search_files(pattern: str, target="content", path=".", file_glob=None, limit=50) -> dict
    target: "content" (search inside files) or "files" (find files by name). Returns {"matches": [...]}
  patch(path: str, old_string: str, new_string: str, replace_all: bool = False) -> dict
    Replaces old_string with new_string in the file.
  terminal(command: str, timeout=None, workdir=None) -> dict
    Foreground only (no background/pty). Returns {"output": "...", "exit_code": N}

Limits: 5-minute timeout, 50KB stdout cap, max 50 tool calls per script. terminal() is foreground-only (no background or pty).

Print your final result to stdout. Use Python stdlib (json, re, math, csv, datetime, collections, etc.) for processing between tool calls.

Also available (no import needed — built into hermes_tools):
  json_parse(text: str) — json.loads with strict=False; use for terminal() output with control chars
  shell_quote(s: str) — shlex.quote(); use when interpolating dynamic strings into shell commands
  retry(fn, max_attempts=3, delay=2) — retry with exponential backoff for transient failures

code.description: Python code to execute. Import tools with `from hermes_tools import terminal, ...` and print your final result to stdout.

- User corrects you or says 'remember this' / 'don't do that again'
- User shares a preference, habit, or personal detail (name, role, timezone, coding style)
- You discover something about the environment (OS, installed tools, project structure)
- You learn a convention, API quirk, or workflow specific to this user's setup
- You identify a stable fact that will be useful again in future sessions

PRIORITY: User preferences and corrections > environment facts > procedural knowledge. The most valuable memory prevents the user from having to repeat themselves.

Do NOT save task progress, session outcomes, completed-work logs, or temporary TODO state to memory; use session_search to recall those from past transcripts.
If you've discovered a new way to do something, solved a problem that could be necessary later, save it as a skill with the skill tool.

   168|
   169|Psychologists who study military service often note its lasting impact on personality traits. High-stress environments, particularly those involving genuine mortal danger, tend to increase conscientiousness and attention to detail. They can also, in some cases, create patterns of hypervigilance and emotional regulation that prove difficult to shed when the uniform comes off.
   170|
   171|Bob Sr. returned from the Pacific War changed. He had seen things, survived things, shouldered responsibilities that no teenager should have to bear. He married Bob's mother in a clandestine elopement—their families would not bless the union because she was Catholic and he was Protestant, and the religious hatred between their households ran deep enough to cut. After World War II, they moved into his parents' partially finished, unheated summer cottage, two young people trying to build a life in a structure meant for vacation weekends.
   172|
   173|Then came the recall.
   174|
   175|When North Korean forces poured across the 38th parallel in 1950, Bob Sr.'s decision to stay in the Naval Reserves—made for sensible economic reasons in peacetime—became a doorway back into war. He served on an aircraft carrier in the Korean conflict, returning to Michigan only after the armistice of 1953. By then, his wife was pregnant with their first child, a boy they would name Robert, after the generations of Roberts before him.
   176|
   177|The GI Bill made possible what would otherwise have been impossible: a small home purchased with a low-cost mortgage, a foothold in the American middle class for a working-class sailor with an elementary school education. In the fall of 1952, Bob was born. A baby brother followed. The family was complete, or so it seemed.
   178|
   179|## The Household Regiment
   180|
   181|Bob's earliest coherent memories of his father are of a man who seemed to exist in a state of perpetual vigilance, as if still standing watch on a carrier deck.
   182|
   183|Saturdays in the Mills household were not days of rest. They were days of chores, of inspections, of tasks assigned with military precision and expected to be completed to military standards. Bob Sr. treated his sons not as children but as sailors—raw recruits who needed to be broken down and rebuilt into capable men. This was authoritative parenting, psychological researchers would later classify it: high expectations coupled with (in theory) strong emotional support. But for young Bob, the firstborn, the emotional support often felt lost in translation, drowned out by the volume of his father's voice.
   184|
   185|That voice. It wasn't that Bob Sr. was angry, not really. Those who understand military training recognize the difference between rage and command presence. Bob Sr. had learned to project authority across engine rooms and flight decks, to make himself heard over the scream of jets and the roar of machinery. When he brought that voice home, he thought he was preparing his sons for a world he knew to be unforgiving. What he didn't understand was that a child is not a sailor, and a living room is not a ship.
   186|
   187|Bob's younger brother resisted the regimen. He would push back, argue, negotiate, refuse. But Bob took a different path. He learned to comply, to anticipate, to internalize the expectations until they became his own. He cleaned his room before being asked. He completed his chores without complaint. He became, in essence, the model sailor his father wanted.
   188|
   189|There was tenderness in Bob Sr., too, though it expressed itself obliquely. The man was a craftsman of extraordinary versatility—electrician by trade, but also plumber, carpenter, model builder. He found his peace in the garage, surrounded by the scent of sawdust and glue, constructing U-control and radio-controlled aircraft from balsa wood and tissue paper. These weren't toys; they were engineering challenges, miniature aircraft that demanded the same precision as their full-sized counterparts.
   190|
   191|The garage became Bob's summer classroom. Under his father's tutelage, he learned to read blueprints, to calculate weight distributions, to understand the aerodynamic principles that kept fragile structures aloft. Other neighborhood boys joined them, drawn by the spectacle of flight and the charisma of a man who could make the impossible seem achievable. Bob Sr. never turned a boy away. The garage became a sanctuary not just for him but for a whole generation of young people seeking the approval of a father figure who demanded excellence and offered, in return, the satisfaction of creation.
   192|
   193|Years later, Bob would recognize this pattern: his father's harshness and his generosity, his demanding nature and his dedication, all facets of a man trying to love his sons in the only language he had been taught. By the time Bob's third brother arrived, fifteen years after Bob himself, Bob Sr. had softened considerably. Experience had taught him that children weren't sailors, that love didn't require drill sergeant volume to be effective. But for Bob, the firstborn, the die had already been cast.
   194|
   195|## The Plate
   196|
   197|If the garage represented Bob Sr. at his best, the dinner table represented something more complicated.
   198|
   199|Both of Bob's parents were overweight—not grotesquely so, not in a way that would have attracted comment in 1950s America, where physical labor was still common and body standards were less exacting than they would become. But they carried the weight of their generation, the legacy of Depression-era scarcity and wartime rationing that had programmed their bodies to treat every meal as potentially the last.
   200|
   201|They also carried the beliefs of their era about parenting. Providing food was love. Making children eat that food was responsibility. And ensuring that nothing was wasted—*clean your plate*—was moral duty inherited from ancestors who had known genuine hunger.
   202|
   203|The problem was that Bob Sr. had no conception of child-sized portions. When he served dinner, he heaped his sons' plates with adult quantities of meat and potatoes and vegetables. And when he said "clean your plate," he meant it literally. His sons would not leave the table until every scrap was consumed.
   204|
   205|Bob's younger brother rebelled. He would sit for hours, stubbornly refusing to finish, willing to endure punishment rather than force down food his body couldn't accommodate. But Bob was different. Bob learned to eat. He cleaned his plate because that was what was expected, what was demanded, what made him worthy of his father's approval. He ate past the point of fullness, past the point of comfort, past the point where his body sent clear signals of satiety.
   206|
   207|Slowly, inevitably, he lost track of what "full" even felt like.
   208|
   209|The psychology of this was complex and would take Bob decades to untangle. His parents would never call him fat—they used the euphemism "husky," as if the word itself could reshape reality. But the reality was that Bob grew up overweight, the product of genetics (both parents were heavy), environment (the forced consumption), and what would later be understood as the early programming of food addiction.
   210|
   211|Neuroscientific research now confirms what Bob experienced instinctively: the brain's reward circuits can be hijacked by eating behaviors established in childhood. When food becomes associated with emotional states—approval, safety, the avoidance of conflict—it ceases to be mere sustenance and becomes a psychological tool, a coping mechanism hardwired into neural pathways before the prefrontal cortex has fully developed.
   212|
   213|Bob's father didn't understand any of this. He was doing what he thought was right, what his own upbringing had taught him to do. He was feeding his sons, ensuring they grew up strong, preparing them for a world that demanded physical resilience. That his methods might be damaging, that he might be programming his firstborn for a lifetime struggle with weight and health and self-image—this never occurred to him. He himself was overweight, locked in his own battles with the scale, unable to recognize the patterns he was passing down.
   214|
   215|## The Weight of Memory
   216|
   217|Looking back across seven decades, Bob can trace a direct line from that dinner table to his adult struggles with food and weight.
   218|
   219|In college, freed from his father's presence, he managed to shed the pounds. The discipline he had learned in the garage—focus, persistence, attention to detail—served him well. He exercised, controlled his portions, found a weight that felt sustainable. For a few years, he was fit.
   220|
   221|Then came career, and marriage, and children, and the inevitable stresses of supporting a family in a high-pressure world. The coping mechanisms he had learned as a child reasserted themselves. Food became comfort again, solace, reward. The weight returned, and with it came the health consequences: high blood pressure, diabetes, the slow accumulation of damage that excess weight inflicts on the human body.
   222|
   223|After his first wife's death, the pattern accelerated. Bob found himself seeking out empty conference rooms at work, scavenging stale donuts left over from morning meetings. The sugar and fat provided momentary relief from grief, from loneliness, from the haunting void of a life suddenly half-empty. These were not conscious choices; they were compulsions, drives encoded in neural circuits laid down decades earlier in a childhood kitchen.
   224|
   225|The professional help he eventually sought revealed the complexity of what he was facing. Food addiction, his therapists explained, was not simply a matter of willpower or character weakness. It was a disorder woven from genetic predisposition, environmental triggers, and deeply ingrained psychological patterns. The memory of his father's voice—*Clean your plate or you will not be able to leave the table*—echoed in his mind not as words but as neural impulses, firing in the reward centers of his brain every time he reached for comfort food.
   226|
   227|Understanding this was the first step toward healing. Bob embarked on a years-long journey of recovery, losing over two hundred pounds through a combination of therapy, exercise, and strict weight management. The battle was never truly won—forty pounds crept back, then had to be lost again—but he learned to see it not as a failure of character but as a chronic condition to be managed, like diabetes itself.
   228|
   229|## The Echoes
   230|
   231|The beep of Sputnik. The chug of his grandfather's locomotive. The roar of his father's voice. The clink of fork against plate in a silent kitchen where a child learned to override his own body's wisdom.
   232|
   233|These memories are not separate strands but a single thread, woven through the fabric of Bob's identity. They represent the intersection of personal history and world history, of individual psychology and generational trauma. The Space Age gave him his dreams; his family gave him the tools to pursue them; and the difficult lessons of his childhood gave him both the drive to succeed and the vulnerabilities he would spend a lifetime learning to manage.
   234|
   235|Bob's father mellowed as he aged, his military bearing softening into something approaching tenderness. He would tell his son, in rare moments of vulnerability, that his mission had been to make Bob a better man than he himself was. In the end, he succeeded—though not in the ways he had planned. Bob became a different kind of father, a different kind of man, learning from his father's mistakes while honoring his intentions.
   236|
   237|When Bob had his own son, he found himself echoing his father's words, but without the yelling. The cycle had come full circle, modified by the wisdom that comes with generational distance. He had internalized the valuable lessons—the importance of discipline, of craftsmanship, of showing up and doing the work—while filtering out the damage.
   238|
   239|This is how memory shapes us: not as passive record but as active participant in the ongoing construction of self. The beep of Sputnik became wonder. The locomotive became heritage. The garage became skill. Even the dinner table, with all its trauma, became understanding—of his father, of himself, of the complex ways that love and damage can intertwine.
   240|
   241|Bob stands now at the intersection of all these memories, looking back with the clarity that age provides and forward with the hope that has sustained him through every challenge. The echoes of 1957 still sound in his mind, but they have been transformed by time and reflection into something richer than mere recollection. They have become wisdom.

   245|# Part Two: The Building
   246|
   247|---
   248|
   249|# Chapter 3: The Garage
   250|
   251|*Where wood, oil, and patience built more than boats*
   252|
   253|## The Smell of Possibility
   254|
   255|You know how some places just feel different the moment you walk in? Like the air itself has a different weight? That's how the garage felt.
   256|
   257|If the dinner table was where my father's Navy training went to die—rigid, oppressive, all about obedience—the garage was where he became someone else entirely. Someone I actually wanted to be around.
   258|
   259|I was ten. Maybe eleven. I don't remember exactly, but I remember the smell. God, that smell. Pine shavings fresh from the planer, sharp and sweet. 30-weight motor oil—that distinctive petroleum tang that clung to your skin no matter how many times you washed. Sawdust everywhere, coating every surface like the world's finest snow. And cigarette smoke. Camel filters, mostly. The smoke would curl up toward the single bare bulb hanging from the rafters while we worked in this silence that wasn't awkward, just... companionable.
   260|
   261|This was the smell of possibility. Of things being built instead of broken. Of knowledge passing from one pair of hands to another without a single order being given.
   262|
   263|My father handed me a hand plane one afternoon. Heavy thing, cast iron, probably made by Stanley back in the '40s. The wood grip was worn smooth from his own hands. I was small for my age—skinny kid, all elbows and knees—and the tool felt awkward, dangerous even.
   264|
   265|"Show you something," he said. Not "Do this." Not "Pay attention." Just... show you something.
   266|
   267|He took a board—pine, maybe a foot long, rough-sawn—and demonstrated. One smooth pass, shaving off a ribbon of wood so thin you could almost see through it. The curl came off like magic, landing on the workbench with a soft whisper.
   268|
   269|"Your turn."
   270|
   271|I gripped it wrong. Too tight. My knuckles white. The first pass gouged the wood, leaving a ugly trench across the grain. I flinched, waiting for the yell, the criticism, the "for Christ's sake, Bobby" that I knew so well from dinner.
   272|
   273|It didn't come.
   274|
   275|He just adjusted my grip. Moved my left hand forward. Shifted my stance so I was balanced. "Feel it," he said. And here's the thing—his voice was different in the garage. Softer. Like he was talking to the wood as much as to me. "The wood will tell you what it wants if you listen."
   276|
   277|That was a different language. Not the Navy language of commands and compliance. This was... I don't know. Something older. The wood had grain, see, and if you went against it, you'd feel the resistance before the tool even bit. You'd hear it in the change of sound, feel it in your hands through the plane's body.
   278|
   279|Competence mattered more than compliance here. Understanding trumped obedience. I didn't know those words then, but I felt it. The garage had its own rules, its own hierarchy, and it operated on a currency I was starting to understand.
   280|
   281|Skill.
   282|
   283|Not rank. Not volume. Not how loud you could yell. Just... could you make the thing work? Could you make it true?
   284|
   285|---
   286|
   287|## The Boat
   288|
   289|The project that would eat up five years of our lives sat in the middle of that garage like a promise. Sixteen feet of mahogany and oak, a wooden boat built from plans my father had ordered from some magazine—I think it was Popular Mechanics, but I'm not certain. Could have been Mechanix Illustrated. They both had those glossy covers with guys in work shirts holding tools.
   290|
   291|It was ambitious. Probably too ambitious for a man with a full-time job at the machine shop and exactly zero formal woodworking experience. But that was part of what made it matter.
   292|
   293|"We're going to build this together," he announced one Saturday morning, spreading the plans across the workbench like a treasure map. The paper was thick, covered in engineering drawings with dimensions in fractional inches—3/16, 7/32, 11/16. All these precise measurements for something that would eventually float on water, where nothing was ever that exact.
   294|
   295|"It'll take time," he said. "Years, probably. But when we're done, we'll have something that floats."
   296|
   297|I remember his laugh at that. Not the polite chuckle he'd give at family gatherings, but a real laugh. The rare kind that came from somewhere deep. It only happened in the garage, away from the pressures of supporting a family, away from whatever ghosts still visited him in the night.
   298|
   299|The boat wasn't practical. Let me be honest—we had no lake house. No trailer. No realistic plan for where this sixteen-foot vessel would actually live once we finished it. My mother pointed this out exactly once, standing in the kitchen doorway with her arms crossed, watching us carry the first oak frames through to the backyard for cutting.
   300|
   301|"Where exactly is this going?" she asked.
   302|
   303|My father just shrugged. "We'll figure that out."
   304|
   305|And that was that. Practicality wasn't the point. I understand that now, in a way I couldn't at twelve. The point was the building. The point was us.
   306|
   307|The frame went up first. White oak, these massive timbers that looked impossibly fragile standing on their own until the ribs went in. They curved like whale bones—there's a cliché for you, but I'm telling you, that's what they looked like. Giving the structure shape and strength.
   308|
   309|I learned to steam-bend wood. You wrap strips of oak in wet rags—heavy cotton rags, the kind they used in the machine shop—and heat them over a washtub of boiling water until they became pliable. Then you bend them around forms before they cool and set into new curves. The physics of it fascinated me, though I didn't have the words for it then.
   310|
   311|How heat could temporarily defeat the structural memory of cellulose. How water acted as a plasticizer. How the wood would hold its new shape once dry, like it had forgotten it was ever straight.
   312|
   313|My father explained none of this in scientific terms. He wasn't that kind of man.
   314|
   315|"Hot water makes the wood lazy," he said, watching me position a rib against the form, holding it with these heavy steel clamps that left marks in the wood we'd have to sand out later. "It forgets it was a straight stick. Then when it cools, it's too tired to remember."
   316|
   317|The explanation was technically wrong. I know that now. Lignin plasticization, glass transition temperature—it's more complicated than wood being "tired." But functionally? It was right. And it captured something essential about how my father thought about the world.
   318|
   319|He was an intuitive engineer. A man who understood forces and stresses through feel and experience rather than formal training. He could look at a structure and know if it was sound, could sense when a joint was weak or a line was true, without being able to articulate exactly why.
   320|
   321|Me? Even then, I wanted to know why. I pored over those plans, studying the engineering drawings, trying to understand the principles behind the design. Why did the ribs need to be on twelve-inch centers? What was the purpose of the keelson versus the keel? How did the lapstrake planking work, each board overlapping the one below like shingles on a roof, creating a hull that was both strong and flexible?
   322|
   323|The questions sometimes annoyed him. I could tell. He preferred doing to analyzing. Preferred the certainty of his hands to the uncertainty of explanation. But he indulged them. Answered when he could. Admitted ignorance when he couldn't.
   324|
   325|And that admission—*I don't know, let's figure it out*—was maybe the most important lesson of all. In the garage, not knowing wasn't a failure. It was an opportunity. Questions led to understanding. Understanding led to skill.
   326|
   327|I didn't know it then, but I was learning something my college professors would never teach me: that expertise isn't about having all the answers. It's about knowing how to find them.
   328|
   329|---
   330|
   331|## The Lessons of Mistakes
   332|
   333|We made errors. Of course we did. I wish I could tell you some inspiring story about how we were naturals, how every cut was perfect, every joint tight. But that's not how it happened.
   334|
   335|A frame piece cut to the wrong length because I'd misread the fractional measurements on the tape. Three-quarters instead of seven-eighths. A simple mistake, but it meant that piece of oak—good oak, quarter-sawn, probably cost my father half a day's wages—was ruined.
   336|
   337|I stood there holding it, knowing what I'd done, waiting for the explosion. This was the part I knew. This was the script. Mistake equals punishment. That was dinner table logic.
   338|
   339|My father took the piece from my hands. Turned it over. Looked at the cut.
   340|
   341|"Okay," he said. "So now we know why you measure twice."
   342|
   343|No yelling. No punishment. Just... analysis. What went wrong. How to fix it. What to do differently next time.
   344|
   345|Another time, a plank split along the grain because we hadn't accounted for the stress of bending it to the hull's curve. Mahogany, this beautiful reddish-brown board with grain like water, and there it was—a crack running six inches up from the bottom edge.
   346|
   347|I was devastated. Actually devastated. I was thirteen, maybe fourteen, old enough to understand what this mistake had cost us. That plank was supposed to be the third strake on the port side. It was supposed to be perfect.
   348|
   349|My father ran his thumb along the crack. Felt its depth. "Wood is forgiving," he said finally. "See this?" He showed me how to fill the split with epoxy and sawdust—sawdust from the same board, so the color would match—turning the flaw into a feature. You could still see it if you knew where to look, a dark line like a scar, but it held. It was strong.
   350|
   351|"Metal isn't forgiving," he told me. "If you make a mistake with steel, you start over. But wood... wood remembers it was part of a tree. It still wants to heal."
   352|
   353|There was wisdom in that I wouldn't fully appreciate until decades later, when I was managing engineering teams and teaching my own children. The philosophy of the garage—iterative improvement, learning from failure, the value of craftsmanship over speed—became foundational to how I approached problems throughout my life.
   354|
   355|But at the time, it was simply how things were done. You measured twice and cut once not because someone had invented that saying, but because wasting a twelve-dollar plank of mahogany mattered when you were living on a machinist's salary. You sanded by hand because power tools left marks that showed through varnish. You took your time because rushing led to mistakes, and mistakes led to rework, and rework meant less time for the project itself.
   356|
   357|I want to tell you something else, something I'm not proud of. There were days I didn't want to be there. Days when my friends were playing baseball or riding bikes or doing whatever normal thirteen-year-olds did, and I was in that garage, sanding the same damn plank for the third time because the grain wasn't quite right.
   358|
   359|I resented it. God help me, I resented it.
   360|
   361|I'd slam the sanding block down. Make noise. Let him know I was unhappy. And you know what he'd do? Nothing. Just keep working. Let me have my fit. Let me learn that the boat didn't care about my mood. The boat only cared about whether the work was done right.
   362|
   363|That was its own kind of lesson. The universe doesn't negotiate. Materials don't care about your feelings. You can be angry at a piece of wood all day long, but it's not going to sand itself.
   364|
   365|Now I understand what he was teaching me. It wasn't just woodworking. It was... I don't know. Resilience? Responsibility? The understanding that showing up matters more than feeling like it?
   366|
   367|I'm still learning that one, honestly.
   368|
   369|---
   370|
   371|## His Mother's Wisdom
   372|
   373|But the garage was only half the story. Maybe less than half.
   374|
   375|While my father taught me to build with my hands, my mother taught me to think with care. To plan before acting. To see the world as a series of interconnected systems where preparation mattered as much as execution.
   376|
   377|"Measure twice, cut once," she would say, watching from the kitchen doorway as my father and I carried boards through to the backyard for cutting. She'd picked up the phrase from her own father, a carpenter who'd built houses during the Depression, and she applied it to everything. Not just woodworking. Decisions. Relationships. The architecture of a life well-lived.
   378|
   379|The phrase became a touchstone for me. A reminder that impulsiveness carried costs that preparation could avoid. My mother embodied this philosophy in every aspect of her domestic engineering. She planned meals a week in advance, shopped with lists, kept a budget written in her neat accountant's hand. Where my father operated on intuition and experience, she operated on systems and forethought.
   380|
   381|One afternoon—I must have been fourteen, maybe fifteen—she caught me in the quiet aftermath of one of those dinner table confrontations that left me angry and humiliated. I was in the living room, I think, pretending to read a book but actually just staring at the same page, boiling with that particular teenage rage that has no outlet.
   382|
   383|She sat down next to me. Didn't say anything for a minute. Just sat there, her hand on my knee, warm and solid.
   384|
   385|"Your father is a good man," she said finally. "But he doesn't know how to be soft. The war made him hard, and his own father made him harder."
   386|
   387|I wanted to argue. Wanted to tell her she was wrong, that he wasn't a good man, that good men didn't yell at their sons for using the wrong fork. But I didn't. Something in her voice stopped me.
   388|
   389|"He's afraid, Bobby," she said. And she used my real name, not the casual "Bob" everyone else used. "Afraid he won't raise you right. Afraid you'll make the mistakes he made. The yelling is fear wearing anger's clothes."
   390|
   391|This was her gift to me. Translation. She helped me understand the man who seemed impossible to understand, decoding the emotional language of a generation that had learned to suppress vulnerability. She taught me that love could be buried beneath harshness, that discipline could coexist with devotion, that the father who demanded so much did so because he cared too much rather than too little.
   392|
   393|I didn't fully believe her then. How could I? I was fifteen, and fifteen-year-olds know everything, which is to say they know nothing. But the seed was planted. And years later, when I was old enough to look back with some distance, I realized she'd been right.
   394|
   395|Not about everything. Maybe not even about most things. But about that.
   396|
   397|She also taught me practical things. Critical things. If the garage was my father's domain, the kitchen was her laboratory, and she made sure I learned my way around it. Not because cooking was women's work—she rejected that notion entirely—but because independence required competence, and competence required practice.
   398|
   399|"A man who can't feed himself is a man dependent on others," she said, teaching me to make an omelet at age twelve. "Your father never learned, and look at him—lost if I'm not there to put a plate in front of him. You're going to college. You're going to live alone. You need to know how to take care of yourself."
   400|
   401|She taught me the chemistry of cooking, though she never used that word. How heat transformed proteins. How acids balanced fats. How the Maillard reaction—she didn't call it that, just said "browning"—turned meat into something transcendent. How to build flavor in layers, starting with aromatics, building with stock, finishing with acid. How to rescue a sauce that had broken. How to tell when bread was done by the hollow sound it made when tapped. How to make a meal from whatever was in the pantry when the grocery money ran thin.
   402|
   403|These lessons carried survival value. When I went to college, I watched classmates gain the "freshman fifteen" eating cafeteria food, then lose it again when they moved off-campus and discovered they couldn't cook. I gained weight too—old patterns reasserting themselves—but I maintained competence in the kitchen, feeding myself well on limited budgets, understanding nutrition in ways that would later support my health journey.
   404|
   405|More than survival, cooking taught me patience. A different patience than woodworking, but related. You couldn't rush a braise. You couldn't force bread to rise. You had to work with the ingredients, understand their properties, respect their timelines. My mother's kitchen operated on the same principles as my father's garage: understand your materials, prepare properly, execute with care.
   406|
   407|I think about her sometimes, when I'm cooking for my grandchildren. When I'm making the same dishes she taught me, using the same techniques, hearing her voice in my head telling me to taste, to adjust, to trust my instincts. She's been gone for years now, but she's still in that kitchen. Still teaching me.
   408|
   409|---
   410|
   411|## The Partnership
   412|
   413|Watching my parents together, I began to understand that their marriage was itself a kind of engineering project. A complex system where two very different people had found ways to complement each other. My father provided and protected, fixed what broke, handled the physical world. My mother managed, planned, maintained the emotional infrastructure that kept the family functioning.
   414|
   415|She moderated him, I realized. When his temper flared at the dinner table, she would intervene—not by contradicting him, which would escalate things, but by redirection. By subtle calibration. By the quiet authority she had established through years of competence. She knew when to let things go and when to step in, when to support her husband publicly and when to talk sense into him privately.
   416|
   417|"Don't judge your father by his worst moments," she told me once. I was sixteen, maybe seventeen, old enough to think I understood everything about disappointment. "Judge him by his consistency. By what he provides. By the fact that he never leaves, never gives up, never stops working for this family."
   418|
   419|She paused. Let that sink in.
   420|
   421|"He doesn't know how to say he loves you. But he shows it every day."
   422|
   423|This perspective—seeing the whole system rather than isolated failures—became essential to my own development as a parent and partner. I learned from her that relationships required translation, that different people expressed care in different languages, that the task of family was to build bridges across those differences rather than demanding uniformity.
   424|
   425|She also taught me resilience, though she would never have used that word. When money was tight, she made it stretch. When my father was difficult, she found ways to manage. When I struggled with school or friendships or the thousand challenges of growing up, she listened without judgment, offered perspective without taking over, believed in my capacity to solve my own problems while remaining ready to help if I asked.
   426|
   427|"I don't want you to be like your father," she said once, surprising me. We were in the kitchen, folding laundry together—this must have been my junior year of high school—and I'd said something about how I'd never yell at my kids the way he yelled at me. "I want you to be like yourself. Take his good parts—his work ethic, his loyalty, his ability to make things. Leave behind the parts that hurt. That's how generations get better. Not by copying, but by selecting."
   428|
